meta.title: F1 numbers and cards: the five scales of an energy system
meta.note: The scale definitions follow curriculum v2 §5.3 (decisions, authority, physics, inputs, outputs). Prairie Town, Prairie Campus, the Plains Grid, Prairie City and Prairieland are fictional; their sizes are illustrative. The real anchors (a U.S. home's average draw, the Southwest Power Pool's 2025 peak, the Lower 48 record hour) are read from 01-power-energy.json and town_days.json, where each carries its source and date.

scales.name: Device and plant
scales.setting: A Prairie Town home, and the wind farm on the ridge
scales.question: What should one site install, and how should it run hour by hour?
scales.who: The owner of the home or plant, within tariffs, codes and connection rules
scales.what: What to install at one site, and how to run it hour by hour
scales.physics: Device ratings, efficiencies, a battery's state of charge, one meter
scales.inputs: Tariffs or prices, weather, connection limits from the host grid
scales.outputs: A load or supply profile, and flexibility at the meter

scales.name: Microgrid and community
scales.setting: Prairie Campus: a college, the county hospital and a rural co-op
scales.question: How do we keep critical services running in an outage, and who owns the system?
scales.who: A campus owner or a rural co-op, under the utility's connection and tariff rules
scales.what: How big to build, which loads stay on when it islands, who owns it, local trading
scales.physics: A campus or feeder network that can island, within protection and voltage limits
scales.inputs: The tariff, the host feeder's export and import limits, outage statistics
scales.outputs: Net load, offers of flexibility, resilience of critical services

scales.name: Regional bulk grid
scales.setting: The Plains Grid: Prairie Town is one node of three zones
scales.question: Will there be enough power, what sets prices, and how should a large new load connect?
scales.who: A grid operator (an ISO, an RTO or a vertically integrated utility), overseen by regulators
scales.what: Which plants run, reserves, new transmission, capacity and connections
scales.physics: A synchronous network: power flow on lines, frequency and inertia
scales.inputs: Aggregated loads and small resources, fuel prices, policy
scales.outputs: Prices, reliability, emission factors, connection timelines

scales.name: City and region
scales.setting: Prairie City (about 250,000 people), its farms, an industrial park and a new data-center campus (a large load)
scales.question: How should a city save, heat, cool, move and power itself, fairly?
scales.who: A city or county (codes, land, transit), with utilities and owners; not power plants or wholesale markets
scales.what: Buildings, heat, transport, land use, local supply, distribution upgrades
scales.physics: Distribution feeders, heat networks, coupling across buildings, transport and power
scales.inputs: Grid prices and emission factors, state and national policy
scales.outputs: Demand trajectories, local siting, distribution needs

scales.name: Nation
scales.setting: Prairieland: five regions, one strait for oil imports, coal-dependent Ridge County
scales.question: Which pathway keeps a nation secure, affordable, clean and fair?
scales.who: A national government and its regulators
scales.what: Targets, instruments, infrastructure, emergency stocks, trade
scales.physics: Energy balances for each region (primary and final), main transmission corridors
scales.inputs: World prices, technology availability, climate commitments
scales.outputs: Policy and price signals, targets and budgets passed down to regions

predict.q: A heat wave is pushing demand toward a record. Who decides which power plants run in the next hour?

cards.text: A homeowner, or a plant's owner, within tariffs and codes
cards.why: One owner decides for one site: what to install behind one meter and how to run it.

cards.text: A campus owner or a rural co-op, under the utility's rules
cards.why: A microgrid's owner sizes it and sets its priorities, but the host utility sets the rules at the connection.

cards.text: A grid operator (an ISO, an RTO or a utility), overseen by regulators
cards.why: The operator of a regional grid commits and dispatches plants and keeps supply equal to demand every moment.

cards.text: A city or county: building codes, land, transit
cards.why: A city controls codes, land use and transit, but not power plants or wholesale markets.

cards.text: A national government and its regulators
cards.why: A nation sets targets, instruments, national infrastructure and trade.

cards.text: What to install at one site, and how to run it hour by hour
cards.why: Rooftop solar, a heat pump or a battery, and their hourly schedule, are one site's choices.

cards.text: How big to build, and which loads stay on when it runs alone
cards.why: Sizing and load priorities in an outage are the microgrid's own decisions.

cards.text: Which plants run each hour, the reserves, new lines and connections
cards.why: Commitment, dispatch, reserves and transmission are decided for the whole synchronous grid.

cards.text: Building codes, heat networks, transit, where solar may go, feeder upgrades
cards.why: These shape a city's demand and local supply over years.

cards.text: Targets, taxes and standards, emergency fuel stocks, trade
cards.why: National instruments set the signals every smaller scale works within.

cards.text: Device ratings, efficiencies, a battery's state of charge, one meter
cards.why: Behind one meter, a model needs the devices themselves, not the network.

cards.text: A small network that can disconnect and run alone, within voltage and protection limits
cards.why: Islanding is what makes a microgrid; its model must know whether the island holds together.

cards.text: A synchronous network: power flow on lines, frequency, inertia
cards.why: A regional grid turns at one frequency, and its lines limit what can flow where.

cards.text: Distribution feeders, heat networks, links between buildings, transport and power
cards.why: A city model couples sectors: heat, transport and power share streets and feeders.

cards.text: Energy balances for each region, the main transmission corridors
cards.why: A national model keeps regions and fuels in balance, not individual feeders.

bins.label: Passed down
bins.sub: a signal or a limit from a larger scale

bins.label: Passed up
bins.sub: a profile or a need from a smaller scale

cards.text: Tariffs and prices
cards.why: A larger scale sets prices and tariffs; a home or campus takes them as given.

cards.text: A connection or export limit
cards.why: The host grid tells a campus or a plant how much it may export or import.

cards.text: National targets and budgets
cards.why: A nation passes targets and budgets down to its regions and cities.

cards.text: A home's hourly load and its flexibility
cards.why: Millions of homes' profiles add up to the demand a grid operator plans for.

cards.text: A campus's net load and its outage needs
cards.why: A microgrid shows the grid only its net load and what flexibility it offers.

cards.text: A city's demand forecast, and where it wants new solar
cards.why: City plans feed regional and national planning.

cards.text: Will it cut my bill under my tariff, and keep the fridge on in an outage?
cards.why: A household weighs its own bill and its own outages.

cards.text: Can it carry the hospital until the generator starts, within the feeder's export limit?
cards.why: A microgrid asks about critical loads and the limits at its connection.

cards.text: Does it lower the cost of the evening peak and supply reserves?
cards.why: A grid operator values batteries for the whole system's peak and reserves.

cards.text: Where would batteries put off a feeder upgrade, and which neighbourhoods gain?
cards.why: A city asks where, and who benefits.

cards.text: How much storage does the national pathway need, and what does it mean for imports?
cards.why: A nation asks about totals, pathways and security.

apply.q: Prairie Campus found the cheapest design for its [[microgrid|microgrid]], assuming it could export all its midday solar. Then the host [[feeder|feeder]] sets an export limit. What happens to the cheapest design?

options.label: Nothing: it was already the cheapest
It changes: for example less solar, more battery, or some solar spilled

feedback.same: The old design breaks the new limit, so it is no longer allowed. A local optimum is only optimal inside its boundary.
feedback.changes: A local optimum is only optimal inside its boundary: a limit passed down from the scale above changes the answer.
feedback.none: Designs that export less still work: the campus can store, spill or build less. The answer changes; it does not vanish.
